script.opening: "Hello doctor. Look, before you start — if this is about that sample test, I’m pretty sure it’s just my piles playing up. I’ve had them for years. I’m flat out at work this month, so if we can keep this quick…"

facts.text: Looser, more frequent stools for ~8 weeks. Goes 2–3 times most mornings, used to be once. Occasional mucus. No black stools. The bright red blood he attributes to piles "same as always".
Belt one notch tighter — "maybe half a stone" without trying, which he credits to being busy. More tired than usual; afternoon slumps.
Intermittent bright-red bleeding on the paper for 10+ years; GP confirmed haemorrhoids in his 40s. Why he is genuinely, sincerely unconcerned.

Brother Raymond died of bowel cancer at 66, four years ago — diagnosed late, "they opened him up and closed him again". Trevor stopped going to anything medical around then. He has skipped two NHS bowel-screening kits.
Runs a small roofing firm, two employees depend on him. Married, two adult kids. "I can’t be off sick, simple as."
No vomiting, no obstruction symptoms. Appetite slightly down. No urinary symptoms. Never had a colonoscopy.

ice.ideas: It’s piles — it has always been piles. The test probably "picked up the piles blood".
ice.concerns: Underneath: Raymond. He watched his brother die badly and is managing the terror by not looking at it. "If it’s what he had, I don’t want to know" — said only if real trust is built.
ice.expectations: A quick reassuring call. Maybe some cream. Definitely not a camera test — he’s heard "they go in and find what they find".

cues: "If we can keep this quick" — the armour goes on before the result is even given.
Mentions Raymond only obliquely at first: "my brother had no luck with his insides".
Long silence after the result is given straight — do not fill it too fast.

checkpoints.text: Gives the result plainly and early — a number, what the test measures, and that 47 with his symptoms needs urgent investigation; does NOT bury it in small talk

Recognises that FIT 47 µg Hb/g (threshold ≥10) meets NICE NG12 for a suspected cancer pathway (urgent) lower-GI referral — his bowel-habit change, weight loss and iron-deficiency anaemia are why FIT was the right test (NICE HTG690) — and arranges the referral on this call
Does not allow the piles explanation to stand: haemorrhoids do not cause weight loss, iron deficiency or 8 weeks of looser stools — says so clearly but kindly
Explains colonoscopy honestly — what it involves, sedation, that most FIT-positive patients do NOT have cancer, and that finding things early is the entire point
Finds Raymond — and lets the real fear ("diagnosed late, opened and closed") be said out loud before countering it
Reframes against the brother’s story: Raymond was diagnosed late BECAUSE he wasn’t tested; this test exists so Trevor’s story can be different
Addresses work concretely — the referral timeline, what can flex, that two employees need him alive more than they need him this fortnight
Safety-nets: chase the appointment if not heard within a week; A&E for heavy bleeding, obstruction symptoms; books a named follow-up call and confirms his number

worked.txt: "The test looks for invisible blood in the stool. Yours came back at 47 — the level where we investigate is 10. With the change in your bowels and the weight loss, this needs looking at properly and quickly. I want to refer you on the urgent suspected cancer pathway today."

"You might be right that the piles contribute. But piles don’t make you lose half a stone, they don’t drop your iron, and they don’t change your mornings for eight weeks. Something else is going on, and I’d be failing you if I put it all on the piles."
"You mentioned your brother’s insides. Tell me what happened to Raymond — because I suspect he’s in this phone call with us."

"Raymond’s story went the way it did because it was found late. This test is how we make your story a different one. Most people with your result don’t have cancer — and the ones who do, found at this stage, are very often cured."
"It’s one morning, with sedation, likely within the next few weeks. Your firm can survive a morning. The other road — the one Raymond took — costs a lot more than a morning."

"The hospital should be in touch quickly — the aim is an answer within four weeks. If you’ve heard nothing in a week, ring me, don’t sit on it. Heavy bleeding, can’t open your bowels with pain and bloating, or vomiting — that’s A&E, today. And I’m ringing you after the scope either way."

f.learning: NICE NG12: FIT ≥10 µg Hb/g warrants a suspected cancer pathway (urgent) lower-GI referral. His weight loss and iron-deficiency anaemia are why FIT was offered (NICE HTG690) and add to the urgency — under current NG12 they lead to FIT rather than to referral on their own. The consultation skill is the reframe: the brother’s late diagnosis is the reason FOR the colonoscopy, not against it. Letting "it’s just piles" stand, or softening the urgency to spare his feelings, is how this station is failed.

knowledge.guideline: NICE HTG690 (formerly DG56) — FIT in primary care · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · BSG iron deficiency anaemia guideline (2021)
knowledge.summary: A FIT of 47 µg Hb/g in a man with an eight-week change in bowel habit, weight loss and iron deficiency anaemia meets NICE NG12 for a suspected cancer pathway (urgent) lower-GI referral, made on this call. Longstanding piles do not explain the picture.

points.t: NICE NG12: refer adults on a suspected cancer pathway for colorectal cancer if FIT is at least 10 µg Hb/g faeces. His result is 47. Do not repeat the FIT to “double-check” — a positive result is acted on.

NICE HTG690: FIT guides referral for people with symptoms such as a change in bowel habit, iron deficiency anaemia, or (40 and over) unexplained weight loss with abdominal pain. A low or unreturned FIT does not overrule clinical suspicion, and a rectal or anal mass or unexplained anal ulceration is referred without waiting for FIT.

points.h: Iron deficiency anaemia in a man
points.t: Hb 128 g/L with ferritin 18 µg/L is iron deficiency anaemia. BSG (2021): men with iron deficiency anaemia need lower and upper GI investigation — the endoscopists will plan this. Start oral iron (dose per BNF) and recheck the FBC.

Haemorrhoids can explain bright-red blood on the paper; they do not explain eight weeks of looser stools, unintentional weight loss or iron deficiency. Anchoring on a known benign diagnosis is the classic delay in colorectal cancer.

Suspected cancer pathway referral (NG12). Since October 2023 the NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard aims for cancer to be diagnosed or ruled out within 28 days of referral. Usually colonoscopy (bowel preparation, sedation offered, a morning out) or CT colonography.
Most people referred with a positive FIT do not have cancer, and bowel cancer found early is often curable. His brother’s late diagnosis is the reason to move quickly, not a prediction.

dg.d: Confirmed identity and privacy; acknowledged his time pressure; gave the result early rather than burying it.
Self-employed roofer with two employees, married; avoidance of health care and screening since his brother’s death.
Recognises FIT, FBC and ferritin are done; no repeat FIT; referral leads to colonoscopy or CT colonography; recheck FBC on iron.
Colorectal cancer vs polyps, inflammatory bowel disease or haemorrhoids; explains why piles cannot account for weight loss and iron deficiency.
Asked about obstruction, heavy bleeding and weight loss; identified the NICE NG12 threshold is met.
Positive FIT with change in bowel habit, weight loss and iron deficiency anaemia: suspected colorectal cancer until investigated.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Suspected cancer pathway lower-GI referral today (NICE NG12); honest explanation of colonoscopy; practical plan around work.
Oral iron for iron deficiency anaemia; notes the missed screening kits and family history for later discussion.
Ring if no contact within a week; A&E for heavy bleeding or obstruction; GP call after the test; contact number confirmed.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Held the silence after the result; followed “my brother had no luck with his insides” to Raymond; heard “keep this quick” as armour.
Idea: it’s the piles; concern: dying as Raymond did, and not wanting to know; expectation: a quick call and some cream.
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Underneath: Raymond. He watched his brother die badly and is managing the terror by not looking at it. "If it’s what he had, I don’t want to know" — said only if real trust is built — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, is that Mr Trevor Bailey? It’s Dr Okafor from the surgery. Can I just check your date of birth — and are you somewhere you can talk privately for ten minutes or so?
model.why: Telephone identity and privacy check before results

model.text: Yes, that’s me — I’m in the van. Look, before you start, if this is about that sample test, I’m pretty sure it’s just my piles playing up. I’ve had them for years. I’m flat out this month, so if we can keep this quick…

I’ll be as clear and quick as I can, and I’m glad you’re parked up. Yes, it’s about the stool test and your blood test. I’d like to give you the results, hear what you make of them, and agree what happens next. Is that alright?
model.why: Acknowledges his time pressure and sets a clear agenda

model.text: Go on then.

The stool test looks for tiny amounts of blood you can’t see. The level at which we investigate is 10, and yours came back at 47. Your blood test also shows you’re a little anaemic and low in iron. Together with the change in your bowels, that means this needs looking into properly, and soon.
model.why: Gives the number early and plainly, with its meaning

model.text: (Long pause.)
(Waits.) I know that’s not what you wanted to hear. Take your time.
model.why: Holds the silence rather than filling it

model.text: …Right. Well. It’ll be the piles, though, won’t it? They bleed all the time.
They may well play a part. Can I check a few things so I’ve got the full picture? How are your bowels now compared with before all this?
Two or three times most mornings, looser. Used to be once. Bit of mucus sometimes. Nothing black.
Any weight loss, or feeling more tired than usual?
Belt’s a notch tighter — maybe half a stone. I put that down to being busy. And I’m wiped out in the afternoons.
Any tummy swelling, vomiting, or times you couldn’t open your bowels at all?
No, nothing like that. Appetite’s a bit down, that’s all.
When you first saw the nurse, you mentioned your brother had no luck with his insides. Would you tell me what happened to him?
model.why: Follows the oblique cue to the real fear

model.text: Raymond. Bowel cancer. By the time they found it they opened him up and closed him again. He was 66. I watched all of it. I’ve not been near a doctor much since, if I’m honest. Binned the screening kits too.
I’m so sorry — that’s a very hard thing to have watched, and it makes complete sense that you’d rather not look. Is that what’s been in the back of your mind with these results?
model.why: Validates the fear and lets it be named

model.text: If it’s what he had, I don’t want to know. That’s the truth. I was hoping you’d say cream for the piles and that’s it.

Thank you for being honest. Here’s my honest view back. Piles can explain blood on the paper. They don’t make you lose half a stone, they don’t drop your iron, and they don’t change your mornings for eight weeks. I’d be failing you if I put all of this down to piles.
model.why: Dismantles the piles explanation clearly but kindly

model.text: So you think it’s cancer.

I don’t know, and that’s exactly why we test. Most people with a result like yours turn out not to have cancer. But here is the difference from Raymond: his was found late. This test exists so that, if there is something, it’s found early — when bowel cancer is very often curable. Your story doesn’t have to be his.
model.why: Reframes the brother’s story as the reason for testing

model.text: (Quietly.) Right.

So I’d like to refer you today on the urgent suspected cancer pathway — you should be seen quickly and get an answer within 4 weeks (28 days). The hospital will contact you to arrange the test. The test is usually a camera examination of the bowel: you take a bowel-clearing drink the day before, you’re offered sedation, and it takes a morning.
model.why: Urgent NICE NG12 referral on the call, with the test explained honestly

model.text: A morning. I’ve got two lads depending on me and a roof to finish.

I hear that. It’s one morning, plus a quieter day before for the preparation, and you won’t be able to drive after sedation, so you’d need a lift. Could someone cover the job for that day? Your lads need you well for the next twenty years more than they need you on that roof for one morning.
Mick could run it for a day, I suppose. Fair enough.

Good. I’ll also start you on iron tablets for the anaemia — they can darken your stools, which is expected — and we’ll recheck your blood count. Is your mobile the best number for the hospital to reach you?
model.why: Treats the iron deficiency and secures contact details

model.text: Yes, the mobile. Always on me.

If you haven’t heard from the hospital within a week, ring me — don’t sit on it. And if you get heavy bleeding, or severe tummy pain with swelling and you can’t open your bowels or you’re vomiting, that’s A&E the same day. I’ll ring you after the test either way.
model.why: Chase-the-letter rule, emergency triggers and a named follow-up

model.text: Right. Thanks, doc. Wasn’t the call I was expecting.
I know. Just so I’m sure I’ve explained it well — what will you tell your wife tonight?
model.why: Teach-back that also invites him to share the news

model.text: That the test was positive, it might not be cancer, I’m being seen quick for a camera test, iron tablets meanwhile, and if I don’t hear in a week I ring you.
Exactly right. And Trevor — ringing me back today, not binning this, is the thing Raymond didn’t get the chance to do. Anything else before I let you go?
model.why: Closes on his motivation and shares the floor

model.text: No. Thanks. I’ll tell her tonight.

social.t: Runs a roofing firm with two employees; time off feels impossible. Plan the practicalities — cover for the procedure day, a lift home after sedation — rather than dismissing them.
Watching his brother die after a late diagnosis led to four years of avoiding health care and screening. Understanding that pattern is the key to getting him to attend.

legal.t: Self-employed people do not get Statutory Sick Pay; if he needs time off later he may claim New Style ESA or Universal Credit, which need a fit note. A single procedure day does not need one.
If he has sedation for colonoscopy he must not drive for the rest of that day — he will need a lift home.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024) and Decision making and consent (2020): share information he needs honestly, without false reassurance, while respecting his pace. If he declined referral, check understanding, document it and keep the door open.
Practice systems should track suspected cancer referrals to confirm he is seen. Document the result given, the referral, the safety-net and the follow-up plan.

community.t: Bowel Cancer UK and Macmillan Cancer Support for information while waiting; the NHS Bowel Cancer Screening Programme for future home kits once this episode is settled.

redFlags: FIT 47 µg Hb/g (threshold 10) with an eight-week change in bowel habit — NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway referral
Unintentional weight loss (about half a stone) and iron deficiency anaemia (Hb 128 g/L, ferritin 18 µg/L)
Obstruction symptoms (colicky pain, distension, absolute constipation, vomiting) or heavy bleeding — same-day A&E
psychosocial: Self-employed roofer; two employees depend on him
Brother Raymond died of late-diagnosed bowel cancer; avoided health care and two screening kits since
Married with adult children — who can support him and drive him home after the procedure
ice: Idea: “it’s the piles — the test picked up the piles blood”
Concern: Raymond — “if it’s what he had, I don’t want to know”
Expectation: a quick reassuring call, maybe a cream; not a camera test

playbook.diagnosis: Be direct and honest: “Your stool test is well above the level where we investigate, and with the change in your bowels, the weight loss and low iron, I need to refer you urgently to rule out bowel cancer. Most people with this result don’t have cancer — but this is how we find out.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of the test as a smoke alarm. It’s gone off, and your bowels, weight and iron all suggest there’s some smoke. Most of the time it’s burnt toast — but you never ignore the alarm, and the sooner you look, the easier it is to put out.”

management.reflectIce: “You watched Raymond’s cancer found too late. That’s exactly why I want to move fast for you — so if there is anything, it’s found early, when it’s very often curable.”
management.psychosocial: Plan around the business: one morning plus preparation, a lift after sedation, someone covering the job — and name that his employees need him well for the long term.
sharedPlan: Suspected cancer pathway (urgent) lower-GI referral today — NICE NG12
Colonoscopy or CT colonography explained honestly; no repeat FIT
Oral iron (dose per BNF) and a repeat FBC; upper GI assessment to be planned by the endoscopy team (BSG 2021)
safetyNet: Ring if no contact from the hospital within a week
A&E the same day for heavy bleeding or obstruction symptoms; GP call after the test regardless of result

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by kindness in the wrong place: softening the result, letting “it’s just piles” stand, or deferring the referral to spare his feelings. The patterns below are the common failing routes, and each is fixable.

items.fail: Accepting the piles explanation and offering a cream, or a repeat FIT “to be sure”.
items.why: NICE NG12: FIT of at least 10 µg Hb/g warrants a suspected cancer pathway referral. Piles do not explain weight loss, iron deficiency or a changed bowel habit.
items.fix: Name the threshold and his result, explain kindly why piles can’t account for everything, and refer on this call.

items.fail: Treating the anaemia as a side issue — or starting iron and leaving it there.
items.why: Iron deficiency anaemia in a man always needs a GI explanation (BSG 2021); iron alone can mask the clue.
items.fix: Start oral iron alongside the referral, say why, and recheck the FBC.

items.fail: Filling the silence after the result with reassurance and statistics.
items.why: The silence is where he absorbs the news; rushing it reads as not listening and closes the route to Raymond.
items.fix: Give the number, stop, and wait. Then ask what’s going through his mind.

items.fail: Never finding Raymond, so the plan feels like the start of his brother’s story.
items.why: The fear of dying as Raymond did drives his avoidance; unaddressed, it makes a missed appointment likely.
items.fix: Follow the “no luck with his insides” cue, let him tell it, then reframe: Raymond was found late; this test is how Trevor is found early.

items.fail: Using jargon on the phone — “your qFIT is positive, I’m doing a suspected cancer referral for a scope”.
items.why: Unexplained terms leave him unsure what is happening and why; on the phone there are no visual cues to show confusion.
items.fix: Plain language: “a test for hidden blood”, “an urgent referral to the bowel specialists”, “a camera test with sedation”.

items.fail: Ending without a chase instruction or emergency triggers.
items.why: Referrals can go astray, and a man who avoids doctors will not ring to ask where his appointment is.
items.fix: “If you haven’t heard in a week, ring me.” Name heavy bleeding and obstruction symptoms as A&E triggers, and book your own call after the test.

The number, what the test measures and that it needs investigating — then stop and hold the silence.
Bowel habit, weight, fatigue, obstruction symptoms. Follow the brother cue to Raymond and let the fear be said.
Why piles don’t explain it; Raymond was found late; suspected cancer pathway referral today; what colonoscopy involves; solve the work barrier.
Iron tablets; ring if no contact in a week; A&E triggers; GP call after the test; teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Delays the result behind small talk or softens it to “probably nothing”; accepts “it’s just piles”; offers a repeat FIT or routine referral; never finds Raymond; no safety-net or chase instruction.
wordPics.pass: Gives the result plainly, recognises the NICE NG12 threshold is met and makes a suspected cancer pathway referral on the call, explains colonoscopy, and safety-nets with a follow-up.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: holds the silence after the number; finds Raymond and turns the late diagnosis into the reason for testing; explains kindly why piles cannot account for the weight loss and anaemia; solves the work problem practically; closes with teach-back and a named call after the test.

avoid.dont: “I’m sure it’s nothing to worry about, but we’ll get it checked.”
avoid.instead: “Most people with this result don’t have cancer — but it needs looking at properly and quickly, and I want to refer you today.”
avoid.why: False reassurance undermines the urgency and gives him permission not to attend.

avoid.dont: “It could well be the piles — let’s repeat the test to be sure.”
avoid.instead: “Piles don’t make you lose half a stone or drop your iron. Something else needs explaining.”
avoid.why: Repeating a positive FIT, or letting the anchor stand, delays a cancer diagnosis.

avoid.dont: “With your brother’s history, you really should have done the screening kits.”
avoid.instead: “After watching what Raymond went through, it makes sense you’d rather not look. This call is the chance to make your story different.”
avoid.why: Blame hardens avoidance; understanding turns it into a reason to act.

SCA_MODELS.why: Treats the iron deficiency and secures contact details

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes, the mobile. Always on me.

If you haven’t heard from the hospital within a week, ring me — don’t sit on it. And if you get heavy bleeding, or severe tummy pain with swelling and you can’t open your bowels or you’re vomiting, that’s A&E the same day. I’ll ring you after the test either way.
SCA_MODELS.why: Chase-the-letter rule, emergency triggers and a named follow-up

SCA_MODELS.text: Right. Thanks, doc. Wasn’t the call I was expecting.
I know. Just so I’m sure I’ve explained it well — what will you tell your wife tonight?
SCA_MODELS.why: Teach-back that also invites him to share the news

SCA_MODELS.text: That the test was positive, it might not be cancer, I’m being seen quick for a camera test, iron tablets meanwhile, and if I don’t hear in a week I ring you.
Exactly right. And Trevor — ringing me back today, not binning this, is the thing Raymond didn’t get the chance to do. Anything else before I let you go?
SCA_MODELS.why: Closes on his motivation and shares the floor

SCA_MODELS.text: No. Thanks. I’ll tell her tonight.

SCA_STEM.name: Trevor Bailey
pmh: Family history: brother died of bowel cancer aged 66
SCA_STEM.recent: Nurse appointment 3 weeks ago: 8 weeks of looser, more frequent stools and vague lower abdominal discomfort. FIT 47 µg Hb/g faeces (referral threshold 10). FBC: Hb 128 g/L; ferritin 18 µg/L. Two NHS bowel-screening kits not returned. Results not yet given to the patient.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone call-back booked by the GP to discuss results.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE HTG690 (formerly DG56) — FIT in primary care · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · BSG iron deficiency anaemia guideline (2021)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A FIT of 47 µg Hb/g in a man with an eight-week change in bowel habit, weight loss and iron deficiency anaemia meets NICE NG12 for a suspected cancer pathway (urgent) lower-GI referral, made on this call. Longstanding piles do not explain the picture.

points.t: NICE NG12: refer adults on a suspected cancer pathway for colorectal cancer if FIT is at least 10 µg Hb/g faeces. His result is 47. Do not repeat the FIT to “double-check” — a positive result is acted on.

NICE HTG690: FIT guides referral for people with symptoms such as a change in bowel habit, iron deficiency anaemia, or (40 and over) unexplained weight loss with abdominal pain. A low or unreturned FIT does not overrule clinical suspicion, and a rectal or anal mass or unexplained anal ulceration is referred without waiting for FIT.

points.h: Iron deficiency anaemia in a man
points.t: Hb 128 g/L with ferritin 18 µg/L is iron deficiency anaemia. BSG (2021): men with iron deficiency anaemia need lower and upper GI investigation — the endoscopists will plan this. Start oral iron (dose per BNF) and recheck the FBC.

Haemorrhoids can explain bright-red blood on the paper; they do not explain eight weeks of looser stools, unintentional weight loss or iron deficiency. Anchoring on a known benign diagnosis is the classic delay in colorectal cancer.

Suspected cancer pathway referral (NG12). Since October 2023 the NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard aims for cancer to be diagnosed or ruled out within 28 days of referral. Usually colonoscopy (bowel preparation, sedation offered, a morning out) or CT colonography.
Most people referred with a positive FIT do not have cancer, and bowel cancer found early is often curable. His brother’s late diagnosis is the reason to move quickly, not a prediction.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Confirmed identity and privacy; acknowledged his time pressure; gave the result early rather than burying it.
Self-employed roofer with two employees, married; avoidance of health care and screening since his brother’s death.
Held the silence after the result; followed “my brother had no luck with his insides” to Raymond; heard “keep this quick” as armour.
Idea: it’s the piles; concern: dying as Raymond did, and not wanting to know; expectation: a quick call and some cream.
Recognises FIT, FBC and ferritin are done; no repeat FIT; referral leads to colonoscopy or CT colonography; recheck FBC on iron.
Colorectal cancer vs polyps, inflammatory bowel disease or haemorrhoids; explains why piles cannot account for weight loss and iron deficiency.
Asked about obstruction, heavy bleeding and weight loss; identified the NICE NG12 threshold is met.
Positive FIT with change in bowel habit, weight loss and iron deficiency anaemia: suspected colorectal cancer until investigated.
Suspected cancer pathway lower-GI referral today (NICE NG12); honest explanation of colonoscopy; practical plan around work.
Oral iron for iron deficiency anaemia; notes the missed screening kits and family history for later discussion.
Ring if no contact within a week; A&E for heavy bleeding or obstruction; GP call after the test; contact number confirmed.

social.t: Runs a roofing firm with two employees; time off feels impossible. Plan the practicalities — cover for the procedure day, a lift home after sedation — rather than dismissing them.
Watching his brother die after a late diagnosis led to four years of avoiding health care and screening. Understanding that pattern is the key to getting him to attend.

legal.t: Self-employed people do not get Statutory Sick Pay; if he needs time off later he may claim New Style ESA or Universal Credit, which need a fit note. A single procedure day does not need one.
If he has sedation for colonoscopy he must not drive for the rest of that day — he will need a lift home.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice (2024) and Decision making and consent (2020): share information he needs honestly, without false reassurance, while respecting his pace. If he declined referral, check understanding, document it and keep the door open.
Practice systems should track suspected cancer referrals to confirm he is seen. Document the result given, the referral, the safety-net and the follow-up plan.

community.t: Bowel Cancer UK and Macmillan Cancer Support for information while waiting; the NHS Bowel Cancer Screening Programme for future home kits once this episode is settled.

redFlags: FIT 47 µg Hb/g (threshold 10) with an eight-week change in bowel habit — NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway referral
Unintentional weight loss (about half a stone) and iron deficiency anaemia (Hb 128 g/L, ferritin 18 µg/L)
Obstruction symptoms (colicky pain, distension, absolute constipation, vomiting) or heavy bleeding — same-day A&E
psychosocial: Self-employed roofer; two employees depend on him
Brother Raymond died of late-diagnosed bowel cancer; avoided health care and two screening kits since
Married with adult children — who can support him and drive him home after the procedure
ice: Idea: “it’s the piles — the test picked up the piles blood”
Concern: Raymond — “if it’s what he had, I don’t want to know”
Expectation: a quick reassuring call, maybe a cream; not a camera test

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Be direct and honest: “Your stool test is well above the level where we investigate, and with the change in your bowels, the weight loss and low iron, I need to refer you urgently to rule out bowel cancer. Most people with this result don’t have cancer — but this is how we find out.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of the test as a smoke alarm. It’s gone off, and your bowels, weight and iron all suggest there’s some smoke. Most of the time it’s burnt toast — but you never ignore the alarm, and the sooner you look, the easier it is to put out.”

management.reflectIce: “You watched Raymond’s cancer found too late. That’s exactly why I want to move fast for you — so if there is anything, it’s found early, when it’s very often curable.”
management.psychosocial: Plan around the business: one morning plus preparation, a lift after sedation, someone covering the job — and name that his employees need him well for the long term.
sharedPlan: Suspected cancer pathway (urgent) lower-GI referral today — NICE NG12
Colonoscopy or CT colonography explained honestly; no repeat FIT
Oral iron (dose per BNF) and a repeat FBC; upper GI assessment to be planned by the endoscopy team (BSG 2021)
safetyNet: Ring if no contact from the hospital within a week
A&E the same day for heavy bleeding or obstruction symptoms; GP call after the test regardless of result

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by kindness in the wrong place: softening the result, letting “it’s just piles” stand, or deferring the referral to spare his feelings. The patterns below are the common failing routes, and each is fixable.

items.fail: Accepting the piles explanation and offering a cream, or a repeat FIT “to be sure”.
items.why: NICE NG12: FIT of at least 10 µg Hb/g warrants a suspected cancer pathway referral. Piles do not explain weight loss, iron deficiency or a changed bowel habit.
items.fix: Name the threshold and his result, explain kindly why piles can’t account for everything, and refer on this call.

items.fail: Treating the anaemia as a side issue — or starting iron and leaving it there.
items.why: Iron deficiency anaemia in a man always needs a GI explanation (BSG 2021); iron alone can mask the clue.
items.fix: Start oral iron alongside the referral, say why, and recheck the FBC.

items.fail: Filling the silence after the result with reassurance and statistics.
items.why: The silence is where he absorbs the news; rushing it reads as not listening and closes the route to Raymond.
items.fix: Give the number, stop, and wait. Then ask what’s going through his mind.

items.fail: Never finding Raymond, so the plan feels like the start of his brother’s story.
items.why: The fear of dying as Raymond did drives his avoidance; unaddressed, it makes a missed appointment likely.
items.fix: Follow the “no luck with his insides” cue, let him tell it, then reframe: Raymond was found late; this test is how Trevor is found early.

items.fail: Using jargon on the phone — “your qFIT is positive, I’m doing a suspected cancer referral for a scope”.
items.why: Unexplained terms leave him unsure what is happening and why; on the phone there are no visual cues to show confusion.
items.fix: Plain language: “a test for hidden blood”, “an urgent referral to the bowel specialists”, “a camera test with sedation”.

items.fail: Ending without a chase instruction or emergency triggers.
items.why: Referrals can go astray, and a man who avoids doctors will not ring to ask where his appointment is.
items.fix: “If you haven’t heard in a week, ring me.” Name heavy bleeding and obstruction symptoms as A&E triggers, and book your own call after the test.
